name: Quincy Jones
description: Quincy Jones is a musician and producer who was raised in Chicago and received the NEA Jazz Masters Fellowship in 2008. His Chicago roots are a documented person-level fact in CultureTechLens's television and film research. Jones composed the theme for the NBC sitcom Sanford and Son, which ran from January 14, 1972 to March 25, 1977 across six seasons and 136 episodes and finished in the Nielsen top ten in five of its six seasons. He also scored and co-produced the 1985 film The Color Purple, directed by Steven Spielberg from Alice Walker's 1982 Pulitzer Prize-winning novel, which was nominated for eleven Academy Awards.

name: Queen Latifah
description: Queen Latifah (born Dana Owens on March 18, 1970, in Newark, New Jersey) is the rapper and actress who carried hip-hop's Afrocentric first wave into the mainstream and then into Hollywood's top rank. Her debut album All Hail the Queen (1989) announced a regal, Afrocentric persona pointedly at odds with the misogyny around her. Her third album, Black Reign (1993), became the first album by a solo female rapper to be certified gold, and its single "U.N.I.T.Y." won the Grammy Award for Best Rap Solo Performance. On television she headlined the sitcom Living Single (1993–1998) as Khadijah James, and on film she broke through in Set It Off (1996) before earning an Academy Award nomination for Chicago (2002). In 1998 she became the first rapper to perform at a Super Bowl halftime show, and in 2023 she was named a Kennedy Center honoree — only the second hip-hop artist so honored. CultureTechLens profiled Latifah in Short #156.

name: Queen Sugar
description: Queen Sugar, created by Ava DuVernay from Natalie Baszile's novel and executive produced by DuVernay and Oprah Winfrey through ARRAY Filmworks and Harpo Films with Warner Bros. Television, premiered on OWN in September 2016 and ran seven seasons — eighty-eight episodes, the final season beginning September 6, 2022 — following the Bordelon siblings' inheritance of a Louisiana sugarcane farm. Its production policy is its monument: DuVernay committed at the start to an all-women directing roster and held it for the entire run — forty-two women directed episodes of the series, thirty-nine of them making their television directing debuts on it, a deliberate pipeline that changed hiring patterns beyond the show itself. It won the NAACP Image Award for Outstanding Drama Series in 2017 and 2022, and the African-American Film Critics Association named it Best TV Drama four consecutive years. Set in the fictional parish of St. Josephine, it treated land — who holds it, who loses it, what it remembers — as the central Black American drama, at the length the subject deserved.

name: Queen Naija
description: Michigan singer and media personality who converted a YouTube audience into a chart career by singing, in public and in detail, about betrayal, motherhood and starting over. Queen Naija Bulls was born on October 17, 1995, in Ypsilanti, Michigan, began singing in church as a child, and first reached national television as a contestant on the thirteenth season of American Idol in 2014. After building a large following as a vlogger, she refocused on music; her single Medicine entered the Billboard Hot 100 at No. 45 in April 2018 and topped the Adult R&B Songs chart. Capitol Records signed her that spring, and follow-up singles Karma and Butterflies each became platinum hits gathered on her self-titled debut EP, which peaked at No. 26 on the Billboard 200. Her debut studio album missunderstood (2020) reached the top ten of the Billboard 200 and No. 1 on the Top R&B Albums chart. She has continued the narrative with the EP After the Butterflies (2023) and the 2025 EP 30., released around her thirtieth birthday.

name: Quentin Richardson
description: Quentin Richardson, born Quentin Lamar Richardson on April 13, 1980, in Chicago, Illinois, is an American former professional basketball player. At Whitney Young High School he led the Dolphins to the 1998 IHSA Class AA state championship and was named a McDonald's All-American. At DePaul he became the only player in school history with 1,000 points, 500 rebounds, and 100 three-pointers, winning both Conference USA Player of the Year and Freshman of the Year in 1999 along with USBWA National Freshman of the Year. Selected 18th overall by the Los Angeles Clippers in 2000, he played thirteen NBA seasons for the Clippers, Phoenix Suns, New York Knicks, Miami Heat, and Orlando Magic, and won the NBA Three-Point Contest at All-Star Weekend in 2005. His career totals are 8,032 points, 3,666 rebounds, and 1,138 assists. After retiring he served as director of player development for the Detroit Pistons (2014–2016) and played in the BIG3. Richardson's teenage years were marked by family tragedy — his mother, grandmother, and a brother all died in 1992, and another brother was murdered in 2005 — which he has spoken about publicly as the ground of his perseverance.

name: Questlove
description: Questlove, born Ahmir Khalib Thompson on 20 January 1971 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, is an American drummer, producer, DJ, filmmaker and author. Raised in a musical family — his father sang as Lee Andrews, fronting the 1950s doo-wop group Lee Andrews & the Hearts — he attended the Philadelphia High School for the Creative and Performing Arts, where he founded the Square Roots with Tariq Trotter, known as Black Thought; the group became the Roots. As the Roots' drummer and joint frontman he helped build one of hip-hop's defining live bands; the Roots have served as the house band for The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon since 2014. He co-founded the websites Okayplayer and OkayAfrica, produced recordings for artists including Common, D'Angelo, Erykah Badu and Jay-Z, and joined New York University's Clive Davis Institute as an adjunct professor in 2016. His directorial debut, Summer of Soul (2021), recovered the filmed record of the 1969 Harlem Cultural Festival and won the Academy Award for Best Documentary Feature and the Grammy Award for Best Music Film in 2022. He is the author of several books, including Hip-Hop Is History (2024).

name: Quinta Brunson
description: Quinta Brunson (born December 21, 1989, Philadelphia) is the creator, executive producer, co-writer, and star of Abbott Elementary, ABC's mockumentary sitcom set in a Philadelphia public school, in which she plays second-grade teacher Janine Teagues. Brunson built her audience herself: her self-produced 2014 Instagram series, The Girl Who Has Never Been on a Nice Date, went viral, and she became a producer and performer at BuzzFeed Video before leaving to build her own work. She attended Temple University and left to pursue comedy. At the 74th Emmy Awards she became the first Black woman nominated three times in comedy categories in a single year and won Outstanding Writing for a Comedy Series; at the 75th she became the first Black woman in more than forty years to win Outstanding Lead Actress in a Comedy Series. Abbott Elementary received a Peabody Award in 2022, and Brunson was named to the Time 100 that year.
